Your horse hauled hard this weekend. Now she's home, eating grain, looking fine from the gate.

But fine-looking and fine-moving are two different things.

Long hauls — especially the kind North Texas competitors put on before summer circuit kicks in — compress the spine, lock up the pelvis, and teach a horse to compensate. She braces for hours just to stay on her feet. That tension doesn't unload on its own.

Dr. Leo looks for it in the first 72 hours post-haul, when the tissue is still responding and an adjustment actually holds. Wait a week and you're chasing a pattern instead of stopping one.

If your horse hauled this week and you're already seeing something off in her movement, this is the window.

DM 'BOOK' to get on Dr. Leo's North Texas schedule.

She used to stand quiet for saddling. Now she pins her ears before the cinch is even close.

Everybody chalks it up to mare-ness, or a bad day, or maybe she doesn't like that saddle pad.

Here's what Dr. Leo actually sees: a horse that hurts. Somewhere in the back, the pelvis, the withers — she's already told you once. The attitude is attempt number two.

By the time the hitch shows up in her stride, she's been compensating long enough that the pattern is dug in. Catching it early — when it's still behavioral, not mechanical — is faster to fix and cheaper to maintain.

If your DFW horse has started acting different before or during work, that's the sign. Don't wait for the limp.

DM 'BOOK' to schedule with Dr. Leo — he comes to your barn.

The summer run schedule doesn't slow down and wait for your horse to feel better.

North Texas competitors are already stacking jackpots, futurities, and WPRA qualifiers between now and fall. The horses putting in that kind of work need to be right behind, sound through the stop, and correct in the lead — every single run.

Dr. Leo is a cAVCA-certified equine chiropractor who works exclusively with performance horses. He comes to your barn. You don't trailer a sore horse — he shows up, does a full assessment, and adjusts on-site.

Barrel horses, rope horses, cutters, ranch horses. If it competes, Dr. Leo has a protocol for it.

Spots on his DFW route fill up as the season heats up. Don't wait until something looks wrong.
